issues.explanation: The profile is for a male patient with police trauma, but two trigger items and the body-shame appraisal are specifically sexual-trauma themed. That is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type unless there is an additional sexual trauma history, which is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.explanation: Within the trigger/appraisal cluster, the content centers on sexual victimization, while the rest of the profile does not describe corresponding sexual-trauma memory content or threat meaning. This makes the selected items clinically incoherent as a single trauma-linked PTSD profile.

issues.explanation: Door/window checking suggests a home-intrusion or generalized safety threat, but the trigger and appraisal content centers on sexualized trauma cues. That threat item is not well linked to the rest of the selected profile and pulls the formulation in a different direction.

issues.explanation: For a police trauma in a 47-year-old male bus driver, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is hard to reconcile unless the index event involved sexual assault or exposure to sexual violence in a highly personal way; nothing else in the profile supports that specificity.

issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is more characteristic of sexual assault or severe bodily violation. In this profile it does not cohere with the police trauma framing, and it is reinforced only by the sexual-trauma-specific trigger, creating an implausible subtheme not supported by the rest of the nodes.

vignette:
Marcus Ellison is a 47-year-old single Black American man who has worked as a city bus driver for nearly fourteen years. He presented for an initial psychological assessment reporting significant distress that has intensified over the past several months, describing sleep difficulties, persistent anger, and a growing sense of isolation from the world around him. His PCL-5 score of 48 places him well within the clinical range for PTSD, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions was one of a man quietly unraveling beneath a surface he has worked hard to keep intact.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Marcus was driving his afternoon route through a commercial district when two police officers boarded his bus in response to a reported disturbance involving another passenger. What followed escalated rapidly. Marcus, who had already begun to de-escalate the situation on his own, was ordered off the bus by the officers and, in the confusion of their commands, was physically restrained against the exterior of the vehicle. He was pushed face-first against the side of the bus, his hands wrenched behind his back, his cheek pressed against the warm metal. He was held there, in full view of his passengers and the street, for what he estimates was several minutes before the officers accepted that he was the driver and not the subject of the call. No apology was offered. He was handed back his keys and told to move the bus along.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus continued working because he needed the income, but something had shifted. Without warning, the image of his own reflection in the bus's side mirror - distorted, pressed flat - would surface in his mind mid-route, arriving with the same physical jolt as the moment itself. Talking about the incident, even in passing, became intolerable; when his dispatcher asked him to file an incident report, Marcus sat with the form for three days before throwing it away. He had come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that nothing would come of telling anyone, that the account would be used against him rather than for him.

His threat monitoring sharpened into something exhausting. At home each night he checked his door locks repeatedly before he could settle - not once, but in circuits, touching each bolt more than he could count. At work, his concentration fractured easily; he missed a stop he had driven for a decade, drawing a complaint that was placed in his file. When a patrol car pulled alongside his bus at a red light, Marcus felt his jaw clench and his knuckles whiten on the wheel. He was certain, in those moments, that the world extended no safety to men like him.

Over the following months, the habits that had felt protective began to cost him in ways he had not anticipated. He stopped attending the Sunday dinners hosted by his church community, a ritual he had kept for years. He avoided the informal conversations with regular passengers that had once been a genuine source of satisfaction in his work. On bad days he would cover his face with his hands in the break room, not wanting anyone to see his expression, and he kept a Bluetooth speaker in his cab, filling the silences with music loud enough to crowd out his own thoughts. He had come to feel that his community - the neighborhood he drove through daily, the congregation he had belonged to for over a decade - was no longer accessible to him, as though the event had placed him on the other side of a window he could see through but not open. People, he had concluded, simply could not be trusted to protect or believe him.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment of rage that frightened him. A passenger questioned his route, and Marcus's response was so sharp, so disproportionate, that he sat in the parking lot afterward shaking, unable to account for himself. He made the appointment the following day. What he said he most feared, sitting in the intake room, was that the person he had been before that afternoon was simply gone. What he hoped, more quietly, was that someone might tell him otherwise.
